summary: This informational document defines requirements for standards on Energy Management, covering monitoring and control functions. Monitoring includes identifying energy-managed devices and components and their power states, inlets, outlets, power, and energy. Control includes functions such as controlling power states.

eli5.summary: This lists what we need to measure and control how much electricity networked gadgets use.

questions: monitoring power use of network devices
how to remotely control device power states
subtitle: Specifications for monitoring and controlling power use in network devices.

tldr.problem: Network devices consume significant energy, and operators lack a standard way to monitor power usage across devices and components, or to control power states to reduce consumption.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines requirements for energy management standards that specify how to identify and monitor energy-related properties (power consumption, power states, battery charge, energy flow) and how to control power states and power supplies of both the monitored device and related upstream devices.
tldr.outcome: These requirements enable the creation of interoperable energy management standards that allow centralized monitoring of power consumption and control of power states, helping operators reduce energy costs and environmental impact.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Requirements for standards specifications, not implementations

today: RFC 6988 is an Informational RFC that defines requirements for energy management standards. Later standards documents (such as MIB modules and IPFIX specifications) have been built on these requirements to enable actual energy management in networks.

sections.title: Energy Management for Network Devices
sections.content:
Energy Management is the practice of measuring and controlling power consumption in network devices and systems to reduce costs and environmental impact. This RFC defines requirements that energy management standards must meet, covering both monitoring (measuring how much power devices use) and control (changing power states to use less power).

The scope includes routers, switches, hosts, and devices connected indirectly through gateways (such as building automation systems). Energy Management functions focus on devices and components that consume electrical energy. A standard that meets these requirements would allow operators to see how much power each device or component uses, track that usage over time, and remotely change power states (for example, sleep or off) to reduce energy consumption while maintaining service levels.
sections.eli5: Network devices use a lot of electricity. This RFC says what a standard needs to measure (how much each device is using) and control (turning devices into lower-power sleep states).

sections.title: Monitoring Energy and Power
sections.content:
Monitoring starts with identifying entities: both entire devices and individual components like line cards or batteries. For each entity, the standard must allow reporting of several categories of information.

Power State describes whether a device is fully on, in sleep mode, or off. Many devices have multiple power states with different power consumption levels. A standard must be able to report the current power state, list all supported states, and provide statistics on how long an entity spent in each state.

Power measurement includes reporting instantaneous power (in watts) and the direction of power flow (received or provided). Standards must also specify the measurement method (direct measurement, estimation based on load, or hard-coded values) and accuracy, since devices vary widely in measurement capabilities. Real power is a minimum requirement; AC power supplies may also require reporting apparent power, reactive power, voltage, frequency, and harmonics.

Energy measurement reports total or delta energy consumed or provided over a time interval (in watt-hours or kilowatt-hours). Standards must support reporting energy per power state and per interface.

Power interfaces (inlets and outlets) must be identified and characterized. A device may have multiple power inlets (fed by different power sources) or outlets (supplying other devices). For each interface, static properties like voltage range and frequency must be reported. For outlets, it is useful to know which inlets of other devices receive power from them, enabling construction of a power distribution topology.

Batteries are monitored separately, reporting charge, charging state, charging cycles, temperature, and capacity. Standards must trigger notifications when battery charge becomes critically low or when replacement is needed.

Time series data (sequences of measurements over time) are important for trending and forecasting. Standards must allow reporting power and energy values at regular intervals, with clear specification of whether values are total, delta, or sliding-window aggregates.
sections.eli5: Monitoring means measuring how much power each device uses right now, what power state it is in, how much energy it used yesterday, which power cables are plugged in, and how full the backup battery is.

sections.title: Controlling Power States and Supply
sections.content:
Energy management is not just about measuring; it also requires the ability to control devices. Power state control allows an operator to command a device to enter a different power state (sleep, on, or off). Not all state transitions are always allowed; for example, you cannot wake a device that is off if it lacks a power button.

Power supply control allows an operator to switch power on or off at a device's power outlet. This is typically used when the device being controlled is upstream in the power distribution tree (such as a Power Distribution Unit or a PoE switch that supplies power to other devices). This is more delicate than local power state control because abruptly removing power from a device can cause damage or data loss.

The RFC requires that the standard support both controlling the entity itself and receiving control commands from other entities that have that capability. For example, a PoE switch can control which of its ports supply power; devices on those ports must be able to report which switch port is supplying them.
sections.eli5: Control means telling a device to go to sleep or turning on/off the power outlet it is plugged into. Some devices can control other devices (like a power strip), so the standard must handle both.

sections.title: Architectural Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC identifies key design considerations for energy management standards. The first is the trade-off between energy savings and service level: reducing power often means reduced performance. A standard must allow policies that optimize this trade-off, keeping some devices fully powered while allowing others to sleep.

A second consideration is local versus network-wide management. Some devices can optimize their own power locally (switching to sleep when idle), while centralized network management can coordinate the power states of many devices (for example, shutting down unused access ports at end of business day). Both approaches have value.

A third distinction is between monitoring and saving. Merely measuring power does not reduce it; measurement is useful for forecasting, planning, evaluating savings strategies, and accounting. Control is what actually reduces energy use.

A fourth important point is that monitoring may occur indirectly via upstream devices. A device without a power meter can still have its power consumption reported by a Power Distribution Unit (PDU) that measures at the outlet. This requires the ability to report information about entities other than the reporting entity, which is unique to energy management.
sections.eli5: Saving power is a balancing act: if you put everything to sleep, users get slow service. Operators can control some devices locally and others from a central system. And some devices get their power measured by the power strip they plug into, not by themselves.

sections.title: Requirements Summary and Security
sections.content:
The RFC organizes requirements into conventional management categories (identifying entities, reporting information, controlling entities) and special energy-management categories (reporting on other entities, controlling other entities). In total, energy management standards must support unique identification and hierarchical reporting (per-device and per-component), multiple classes of power states with state statistics, measurement of power with method and accuracy metadata, energy measurement with time series support, battery status, and both direct control and control through upstream devices.

Security is paramount because power control can disrupt networks. All control actions (setting power states and switching power supplies) must be protected by authentication, authorization, and integrity checking. Monitoring data is also sensitive because detailed power patterns can reveal operational information. Standards must require confidentiality, authenticity, and access control for monitored data. The RFC also recognizes that some devices are not secure enough to be directly Internet-facing and must be isolated behind gateways that enforce security policies.
sections.eli5: The standard must track which device is which, what power state each is in, how much power it uses, and let the operator control power states. But changing power state is risky, so all control commands must be authenticated and encrypted.
